pos: n. (the first daughter house of Cîteaux, founded 1113 on the Grosne in Burgundy)
etymology: French la ferté, the stronghold, from Latin firmitas, firmness.
biblical_def: La Ferté-sur-Grosne was the first daughter of Cîteaux, founded in 1113 when the mother house, newly revived under Stephen Harding and swollen by Bernard's arrival, had more monks than it could feed. It was followed by Pontigny in 1114 and by Clairvaux and Morimond in 1115, and these four are the elder daughters from whom every later Cistercian house descends. Under the Charter of Charity the abbot of La Ferté was one of the four who visited Cîteaux itself, so that even the mother house stood under correction. The abbey was wrecked at the Revolution and little survives beyond the abbot's lodging. This dictionary records La Ferté for the principle its founding embodies. A house that grows beyond its means does not hoard; it sends, and Scripture shows the pattern when the land cannot hold the company, “the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together” (Gen 13:6). Growth itself is God's doing rather than the planter's, “but God that giveth the increase” (1Co 3:7). And the mutual visitation that bound the four is simply accountability built into a constitution, “Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend” (Pro 27:17), “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour” (Ecc 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a colony as a company transplanted from the mother country; to plant as to settle; increase as augmentation; visitation as the inspection of a superior; and a daughter as a female descendant, used figuratively of dependent towns.
webster_full: COLONY, n. A company of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province or country, and remaining subject to the jurisdiction of the parent state.
PLANT, v.t. To set in the ground for growth; to settle; to fix the first inhabitants; to introduce and establish.
INCREASE, n. Augmentation; a growing larger; extension; also, produce; profit; interest.
VISITATION, n. The act of a superior or superintending officer, who visits a corporation or religious house to examine into the manner in which it is conducted.
DAUGHTER, n. A female descendant; in Scripture, the inhabitants of a city or country; also, a dependent town.
scriptures: Gen 13:6
And the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together: for their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together.
So then neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
corruption_summary: The first daughter of Cîteaux, 1113: a crowded house that sent rather than hoarded, and a constitution that put even the mother under visitation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is sending. Cîteaux did not build a larger dormitory; it sent twelve monks and an abbot to found a new house, and did it three more times within three years. The pattern is older than the Cistercians, “the land was not able to bear them” (Gen 13:6), and the increase that forces the decision belongs to God, “neither is he that planteth any thing, neither he that watereth” (1Co 3:7).

The second principle is mutual correction written into the structure. The Charter of Charity made the four elder abbots visitors of Cîteaux itself, so that the founding house could be reproved by its own children. Scripture gives the reason such arrangements work, “Iron sharpeneth iron” (Pro 27:17), and the plain arithmetic behind them, “Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9). Any eldership that cannot be corrected by anyone has made a different arrangement than the one Stephen Harding wrote.

“but God that giveth the increase” (1Co 3:7) — who filled Cîteaux in the first place.
“Iron sharpeneth iron” (Pro 27:17) — four abbots appointed to correct their own mother.

pos: n. (the second daughter of Cîteaux, founded 1114 in the Yonne, refuge of three exiled archbishops of Canterbury)
etymology: From the Gallo-Roman place name Pontiniacum, the estate of Pontinius, by the bridge over the Serein.
biblical_def: Pontigny was founded in 1114 as the second daughter of Cîteaux, on the Serein in the Yonne, and its church is the largest Cistercian church still standing: a vast, almost unornamented nave that shows better than any text what the order meant by plainness. Its peculiar fame is as a place of refuge. Three archbishops of Canterbury in exile from English kings were sheltered there, Thomas Becket for two years from 1164, Stephen Langton during the interdict, and Edmund of Abingdon, who died nearby in 1240 and whose shrine the abbey kept. This dictionary records Pontigny chiefly for that ministry, because sanctuary for the hunted is a thing Scripture commands rather than merely permits. The law appointed cities for the man who had to flee, “that the slayer may flee thither” (Num 35:11), and the prophet makes the sheltering of the outcast a test of real religion, “hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth” (Isa 16:3). God himself is named the refuge, “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1), and the open door for a stranger is commanded of his people, “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines refuge as shelter or protection from danger; an exile as one banished from his country; sanctuary as a sacred place giving protection; an outcast as one driven out; and asylum as a place of retreat and security.
webster_full: REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects from danger, distress or calamity.
EXILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; also, the person banished.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; particularly among the Israelites, the most retired part of the temple; also, a place of protection; a sacred asylum.
OUTCAST, n. One who is cast out or expelled; an exile; one driven from home or country.
ASYLUM, n. A sanctuary or place of refuge, where criminals and debtors shelter themselves from justice; any place of retreat and security.
scriptures: Then ye shall appoint you cities to be cities of refuge for you; that the slayer may flee thither, which killeth any person at unawares.
Isa 16:3
Take counsel, execute judgment; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth.
Psa 46:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
corruption_summary: The second daughter of Cîteaux, 1114: the largest Cistercian church standing, and a sanctuary that sheltered three exiled archbishops.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is sanctuary for the hunted. The law of Moses does not leave the fugitive to the mercy of whoever reaches him first; it builds him somewhere to run, “that the slayer may flee thither” (Num 35:11). Isaiah makes hiding the refugee a test of a nation's counsel, “hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth” (Isa 16:3). A church that will not shelter anyone has misplaced something.

Pontigny's plainness is the second thing worth keeping. The order forbade towers, coloured glass, and carved capitals, and the result at Pontigny is a building whose proportions do the work that ornament usually does. The impulse was right even where the rule that produced it was arbitrary, because the refuge Scripture names is a person rather than a place, “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1), and the door that matters is the one opened to a stranger, “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2).

“hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth” (Isa 16:3) — what Pontigny did for three archbishops.
“God is our refuge and strength” (Psa 46:1) — the refuge no abbey can replace.

pos: n. (c. 1085–1148, Benedictine abbot who resigned to become a Cistercian, theologian of love and opponent of Abelard)
etymology: William, from Germanic wil, will, and helm, helmet; of Saint-Thierry, his abbey near Reims.
biblical_def: William was born at Liège, became a Benedictine, and in 1120 was made abbot of Saint-Thierry near Reims. He wanted to be a plain Cistercian monk and Bernard of Clairvaux told him twice to stay where he was; in 1135 he resigned anyway and entered the Cistercian house at Signy, where he wrote until his death in 1148. His best-known work is the Golden Epistle, written to the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu, and his most consequential act was detecting and attacking the errors in Abelard's teaching on the Trinity and the atonement, which he brought to Bernard's notice and which led to Abelard's condemnation at Sens. This dictionary records William for a doctrinal instinct worth having. He treated error about the person and work of Christ as a thing to be named rather than debated politely, which is what Scripture requires, “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). His theology of love is likewise grounded where Scripture grounds it, in God's initiative rather than ours, “We love him, because he first loved us” (1Jo 4:19), and in a love that is the fruit of his Spirit, “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost” (Rom 5:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines doctrine as what is taught; heresy as a fundamental error in religion; to contend as to strive in debate; love as strong affection; and contemplation as holy meditation on sacred things.
webster_full: DOCTRINE, n. Principles or positions in any science; whatever is taught; the act of teaching; in theology, the truths of the gospel.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
CONTEND, v.i. To strive in debate; to dispute earnestly; to strive in opposition; to struggle for.
LOVE, n. An affection of the mind excited by beauty and worth of any kind, or by the qualities of an object which communicate pleasure.
CONTEMPLATION, n. Holy meditation; attention to sacred things; a particular attention to the subject of our salvation.
scriptures: Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
We love him, because he first loved us.
Rom 5:5
And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.
corruption_summary: Abbot turned simple monk, c. 1085–1148: wrote the Golden Epistle, and named Abelard's errors when it would have been easier to admire him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of naming error in doctrine. William read Abelard carefully, saw what the teaching did to the Trinity and the atonement, and said so in writing to a man who could act. Scripture frames that duty as a contest rather than a courtesy, “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3), and makes it part of the qualification for office, “to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9).

The second thing to keep is the order of love in his theology. William does not begin with the soul's ascent but with God's descent, which is where John begins, “We love him, because he first loved us” (1Jo 4:19), and where Paul locates the supply, “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us” (Rom 5:5). A mysticism that starts with the climber ends in despair or in pride; one that starts with the gift can end in neither.

Greek elegcho (G1651) — to convict, to refute an opponent; “to exhort and to convince the gainsayers”, Titus 1:9.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, healthy, of doctrine; “by sound doctrine”, Titus 1:9.
Greek agapao (G25) — to love, here answering a prior love; “We love him, because he first loved us”, 1 John 4:19.
Greek ekcheo (G1632) — to pour out abundantly; “the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts”, Romans 5:5.
usage: “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — why he wrote against Abelard.
“to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — part of the office, not a failure of charity.
“We love him, because he first loved us” (1Jo 4:19) — the order his theology of love keeps.

pos: n. (1110–1167, English Cistercian abbot of Rievaulx, author of Spiritual Friendship)
etymology: Aelred, Old English Æthelræd, noble counsel; of Rievaulx in the North Riding.
biblical_def: Aelred was born at Hexham, son and grandson of married priests of the old English church, and was raised at the court of David I of Scotland, where he rose to be steward. About 1134 he turned aside to the new Cistercian house at Rievaulx in Yorkshire and stayed; he was made abbot in 1147 and governed some six hundred and fifty men until his death in 1167. His writings are unusually warm for the century: the Mirror of Charity, a life of Edward the Confessor, and above all Spiritual Friendship, which takes Cicero's treatise and rebuilds it on Christ. This dictionary records Aelred because the subject he made his own is one the Bible treats seriously and the church often does not. Scripture gives friendship a definition with a cost in it, “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Pro 17:17), and a ceiling, “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13). It names such a bond at its height, “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David” (1Sa 18:1), and insists the honesty in it will sometimes hurt, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines friendship as attachment to a person proceeding from esteem; a friend as one attached by affection; affection as a bent of mind toward a particular object; charity as love and good will; and adversity as a state of affliction.
webster_full: FRIENDSHIP, n. An attachment to a person, proceeding from intimate acquaintance, and a reciprocation of kind offices, or from a favorable opinion of the amiable and respectable qualities of his mind.
FRIEND, n. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection, which lead him to desire his company.
AFFECTION, n. A bent of mind towards a particular object, holding a middle place between disposition and passion.
CHARITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will; a disposition of heart which inclines men to think favorably of their fellow men.
ADVERSITY, n. An event or series of events which oppose success or desire; misfortune; calamity; affliction; distress.
scriptures: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
And it came to pass, when he had made an end of speaking unto Saul, that the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
Pro 27:6
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
corruption_summary: Cistercian abbot of Rievaulx, 1110–1167: wrote the century's best book on friendship and governed six hundred men with it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that friendship is a serious Christian subject with a biblical shape. Scripture makes constancy the test rather than enjoyment, “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Pro 17:17), and lets the Lord set the measure at the only place it can finally be set, “that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13). Aelred was right that a cloister full of men needs this taught, and so does a congregation.

The live distortion is a sentimental friendship that cannot say anything hard. Aelred insisted that a friend who flatters is no friend, which is Solomon's own position, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6). The great biblical instance involves a man surrendering a throne to the friend who would take it, “the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David” (1Sa 18:1). That is costly and clear-eyed, and it is not what most people mean by the word.

roots_lines: Hebrew rea' (H7453) — a friend, a companion; “A friend loveth at all times”, Proverbs 17:17.
Hebrew tsarah (H6869) — distress, the brother's proper hour; “a brother is born for adversity”, Proverbs 17:17.

“that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13) — the ceiling Aelred would not lower.
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Pro 27:6) — why flattery disqualifies.

pos: n. (c. 1100–1169, English-born Cistercian abbot of Stella in Poitou, preacher and theologian of the soul)
etymology: Isaac, from Hebrew Yitschaq, he laugheth; of Stella, French L'Étoile, the star.
biblical_def: Isaac was an Englishman, educated probably at Paris under the best masters of the day, who became a Cistercian and was abbot of Stella, or L'Étoile, near Poitiers from about 1147. He left fifty-five sermons and two short treatises, On the Soul and On the Office of the Mass, and he is the most philosophically trained of the twelfth-century Cistercians, which made him uneasy among men who distrusted the schools. He ended his life on the island of Ré, in a hard and obscure foundation. This dictionary records Isaac because his central concern, the nature of the soul and its restoration to the image of God, is where Scripture itself begins and ends on the subject of man. Man is made in that image, “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him” (Gen 1:27), and the image is being renewed in knowledge, “renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him” (Col 3:10). The end of the work is conformity to the Son, “predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom 8:29), and the sight that completes it is promised, “we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” (1Jo 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the soul as the spiritual, rational and immortal substance in man; the image as a representation or likeness; to renew as to make new again; conformity as likeness or correspondence; and likeness as resemblance in form.
webster_full: SOUL, n. The spiritual, rational and immortal substance in man, which distinguishes him from brutes; that part of man which enables him to think and reason.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; also, an idea; a representation in the mind.
RENEW, v.t. To renovate; to restore to a former state, or to a good state, after decay or depravation; to make new.
CONFORMITY, n. Likeness; correspondence with a model or pattern; agreement; harmony.
LIKENESS, n. Resemblance in form; similitude; also, one who resembles another; an image.
scriptures: Gen 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Col 3:10
And have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him:
Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is.
corruption_summary: English Cistercian abbot in Poitou, c. 1100–1169: a trained mind among men who distrusted the schools, writing on the soul and the image of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the image of God is the right frame for every question about what a man is. Scripture states it at the outset without qualification, “in the image of God created he him” (Gen 1:27), and treats salvation as the repair of that image rather than the issue of a ticket, “renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him” (Col 3:10).

The second thing Isaac's career illustrates is the uneasy place of a trained mind in a movement that prizes simplicity. The Cistercians were suspicious of the schools, and Isaac was a schoolman who had become a monk. Scripture does not oppose learning to devotion; it makes the end of the whole process a likeness that is God's own purpose, “predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom 8:29), and a sight that will finish what study began, “we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” (1Jo 3:2).

pos: n. (c. 1085–1159, Limousin hermit and founder of Obazine, affiliated to Cîteaux in 1147)
etymology: Stephen, from Greek stephanos, a crown; Obazine, a place name of the Corrèze.
biblical_def: Stephen was a priest of the Limousin who about 1124 went with a companion into the forest of Obazine to live as a hermit. Others came, as they always did; he built, organised, and found himself governing a community of men and, nearby, a house of women, which was unusual and which he refused to abandon. In 1147 he brought the whole foundation under Cîteaux, and Obazine became a Cistercian abbey with its sister house of Coyroux still in its care. He was a builder of roads and bridges as well as of cloisters, and the aqueduct his monks cut into the cliff face still carries water. This dictionary records Stephen because his career answers a question the solitary life always raises: what happens when the hermit is found? Scripture's answer is that he is not permitted to stay hidden, because a city on a hill cannot be, “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14). The gift he was given was for others, “minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1Pe 4:10), and the care he would not drop is what pure religion is said to look like, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27), “Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hermit as a solitary living in seclusion; a founder as one who establishes; to minister as to serve or supply; a burden as that which is borne with labour; and a steward as one who manages for another.
webster_full: HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret; a beadsman.
FOUNDER, n. One that founds, establishes and erects; one that begins, or lays a foundation; one from whom any thing originates.
MINISTER, v.t. To give; to afford; to supply; to serve in any office or duty; to attend and serve.
BURDEN, n. That which is borne or carried; a load; that which is grievous, wearisome or oppressive.
STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and receive and pay money.
scriptures: Mat 5:14
Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Gal 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
corruption_summary: Limousin hermit turned abbot, c. 1085–1159: found in his forest, he built roads, an aqueduct and a house of women he refused to abandon.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the solitary who is discovered is not thereby interrupted; he is assigned. Stephen went to the forest for himself and spent thirty-five years on other people, which is the normal course. Scripture states the impossibility of staying hidden when God intends otherwise, “A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mat 5:14), and makes every gift a trust held for others, “As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another” (1Pe 4:10).

The second thing is his refusal to drop the women's house. Affiliating to Cîteaux would have been simpler without Coyroux, and the order was reluctant; he kept it. Pure religion in James is defined by exactly that kind of inconvenient care, “To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27), and the law of Christ is fulfilled by carrying what is not yours to carry, “Bear ye one another's burdens” (Gal 6:2).

“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27) — the house he would not give up.
“Bear ye one another's burdens” (Gal 6:2) — the law he was actually keeping.

pos: n. (c. 1083–1136, fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, author of the Customs of the Carthusians)
etymology: A Dauphinois form of the Germanic name Wido, wood or wide.
biblical_def: Guigo, usually called Guigo I to distinguish him from the later prior of the same name, governed the Grande Chartreuse from 1109 to 1136 and is the real organiser of the Carthusian order. Bruno had left no rule; Guigo was asked by other houses what the usage of the Chartreuse actually was, and about 1127 he wrote the Consuetudines Cartusiae, which fixed the solitary cell, the common office, the silence, the diet and the copying of books, and which the order has kept with remarkably little change for nine centuries. He also left a book of Meditations, short and unsparing. The ladder of four rungs that made the Carthusians famous, reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation, belongs to the later Guigo II. This dictionary records Guigo I for the care of books the Customs required, since he ordered every monk supplied with writing materials and told them they could preach with their hands what they could not preach with their mouths. Scripture puts the same weight on written witness, “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2), “What thou seest, write in a book” (Rev 1:11), and on reading that shapes a life, “in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2), “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines custom as established practice; a prior as the superior of a convent; meditation as close or continued thought; to copy as to transcribe; and silence as forbearance of speech.
webster_full: CUSTOM, n. Frequent or common use, or practice; a frequent repetition of the same act; established usage having the force of law.
PRIOR, n. The superior of a convent of monks, or one next in dignity to an abbot.
MEDITATION, n. Close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind; serious contemplation.
COPY, v.t. To write, print or engrave according to an original; to form a like work by writing.
SILENCE, n. Forbearance of speech in man; taciturnity; omission of speech.
scriptures: Hab 2:2
And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.
Rev 1:11

Saying, I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last: and, What thou seest, write in a book, and send it unto the seven churches which are in Asia; unto Ephesus, and unto Smyrna, and unto Pergamos, and unto Thyatira, and unto Sardis, and unto Philadelphia, and unto Laodicea.
Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.
corruption_summary: Fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, c. 1083–1136: wrote the Customs that still govern the order, and set every silent monk to copying books.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Guigo put in the Customs: men vowed to silence were to preach with their hands. The copying of books was not a hobby of the cell but its public ministry. Scripture gives the practice its charter, “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2), and repeats the command to the last apostle, “What thou seest, write in a book” (Rev 1:11).

The second thing to keep is the discipline of continuous meditation, which the Carthusian day was built around. The psalms describe it without any mystical apparatus at all: a man delighting in the law and turning it over at all hours, “in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2), and storing it where it will do its work on him, “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11). The aim is not an experience but a changed man.

Hebrew luach (H3871) — a tablet for a running reader; “that he may run that readeth it”, Habakkuk 2:2.
Greek grapho (G1125) — to write, by direct command; “What thou seest, write in a book”, Revelation 1:11.
Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to murmur, to muse continually; “in his law doth he meditate day and night”, Psalm 1:2.
Hebrew tsaphan (H6845) — to hide, to store up as treasure; “Thy word have I hid in mine heart”, Psalm 119:11.
usage: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables” (Hab 2:2) — the charter for a silent man with a pen.
“in his law doth he meditate day and night” (Psa 1:2) — the Carthusian day, stated in a psalm.
“that I might not sin against thee” (Psa 119:11) — what the storing is for.

pos: n. (c. 292–348, Egyptian founder of cenobitic monasticism and author of the first monastic rule)
etymology: From Coptic pakhom, the eagle or falcon; latinised as Pachomius.
biblical_def: Pachomius was an Egyptian conscripted into the Roman army as a young man and shut up in a prison at Thebes, where Christians brought food to the conscripts without being asked. He never forgot it. Released, he was baptised, spent years under an older hermit, and about 320 founded at Tabennisi on the Nile the first community of monks living under a common rule, a wall, a timetable and a superior, rather than scattered in separate caves. By his death in 348 there were nine houses of men and two of women, numbering thousands. His rule, later translated into Latin by Jerome, lies behind Basil and behind Benedict. This dictionary records Pachomius because the thing that converted him is the thing the New Testament says will, and because his invention answers a real danger in solitude. Unasked kindness to strangers is what he saw, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35), and love is the mark Christ appointed, “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another” (Joh 13:35). The common life he built has Scripture behind it, “all that believed were together, and had all things common” (Act 2:44), and the plain argument of Ecclesiastes, “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a monastery as a house for religious retirement; a rule as a prescribed method of conduct; a community as a society having common rights; kindness as good will and beneficence; and a stranger as a foreigner or one unknown.
webster_full: MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from ordinary temporal concerns, whether an abbey, a priory or a nunnery.
RULE, n. A prescribed form or method of conduct; a maxim, canon or precept to be observed.
COMMUNITY, n. Common possession; as a community of goods; also, society at large, or a body of people having common rights.
KINDNESS, n. Good will; benevolence; that temper or disposition which delights in contributing to the happiness of others.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one unknown; a guest.
scriptures: For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
Act 2:44
And all that believed were together, and had all things common;
Ecc 4:12
And if one prevail against him, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
corruption_summary: Egyptian soldier turned founder, c. 292–348: converted by unasked kindness in a prison, he gave the solitaries a wall, a rule and a timetable.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the thing that actually converted him. Christians fed conscripted strangers who could do nothing for them, and a young pagan soldier noticed. That is precisely the sentence Christ puts in the mouth of the king at the judgment, “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35), and the sign he appointed for his own, “if ye have love one to another” (Joh 13:35). No argument reached Pachomius; a meal did.

His invention also corrects something real. The Egyptian desert was full of solitaries with no one to tell them they were wrong, and eccentricity and pride flourished there. A community under a rule puts a man where he can be contradicted. Scripture assumes that setting, “all that believed were together, and had all things common” (Act 2:44), and gives the reason plainly, “a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12). The remaining error is the wall itself, which Scripture never builds.
roots_summary: Greek xenos (G3581), a stranger; Greek agape (G26), love; Greek koinos (G2839), common; Hebrew chebel (H2256), a cord; Greek sunago (G4863), to gather in.
roots_lines: Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger, the one taken in; “I was a stranger, and ye took me in”, Matthew 25:35.
Greek peinao (G3983) — to hunger, the prisoner's condition; “For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat”, Matthew 25:35.
Greek mathetes (G3101) — a disciple, known by a mark; “By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples”, John 13:35.
Greek koinos (G2839) — common, shared in a body; “all that believed were together, and had all things common”, Acts 2:44.
Hebrew chebel (H2256) — a cord, strong in the plaiting; “a threefold cord is not quickly broken”, Ecclesiastes 4:12.
usage: “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35) — the kindness that converted a conscript.
“if ye have love one to another” (Joh 13:35) — the mark he saw before he believed.
“a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecc 4:12) — why he walled the solitaries in together.

pos: n. (c. 747–821, Frankish reformer who made the Rule of Benedict the single standard of western monasticism)
etymology: Benedict, Latin Benedictus, blessed; of Aniane, his abbey in Languedoc.
biblical_def: Born Witiza, a Visigothic nobleman at the court of Pepin and Charlemagne, he nearly drowned saving his brother, left the court, and became a monk of extreme severity before founding his own house at Aniane about 780. Louis the Pious brought him north and gave him authority over the monasteries of the empire, and at the councils of Aachen in 816 and 817 he imposed the Rule of Benedict as the single standard everywhere, with a uniform set of customs attached. Before him a Frankish monastery might follow any of a dozen rules or a mixture; after him there was one, which is why the whole later West is Benedictine. This dictionary records him as the second Benedict for a reason worth weighing. Uniformity is a real good, and Scripture values order and common practice in the churches, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40), “we have no such custom, neither the churches of God” (1Co 11:16). But uniformity imposed by an emperor's officer is a different thing from unity in the truth, “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3), and the standard a church is actually bound to is not a rule but a word, “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines uniformity as conformity to one pattern; reform as amendment of what is corrupt; a council as an assembly convened for consultation; custom as established usage; and a standard as that which is established as a rule or model.
webster_full: UNIFORMITY, n. Resemblance to itself at all times; consistency; sameness; conformity to one rule or mode.
REFORM, n. A reformation; amendment of what is defective, vicious, corrupt or depraved.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
CUSTOM, n. Frequent or common use, or practice; established usage having the force of law.
STANDARD, n. That which is established by sovereign power as a rule or measure; a criterion; a test.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
But if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, neither the churches of God.
Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: The second Benedict, c. 747–821: gave the West one monastic rule by imperial authority, and showed the difference between uniformity and unity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that order is not the enemy of life. Paul closes a chapter on disorderly worship with a plain requirement, “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40), and is willing to appeal to settled practice across the churches as an argument, “we have no such custom, neither the churches of God” (1Co 11:16). Benedict of Aniane was not wrong to want the houses to stop improvising.

The caution is in the instrument. He achieved his reform through an emperor's authority, which produced conformity quickly and could not produce agreement. Scripture puts the labour where the result actually lies, “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3), and fixes the only standard that can finally settle a dispute, “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20). A rule enforced by the state is held only as long as the state holds it, and within a century the houses had slipped again.

Greek sunetheia (G4914) — a settled custom of the churches; “we have no such custom, neither the churches of God”, 1 Corinthians 11:16.
Greek henotes (G1775) — oneness, unity to be kept; “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace”, Ephesians 4:3.
Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to make haste, to labour at; “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit”, Ephesians 4:3.
Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, the appointed standard; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.
usage: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the good his reform was reaching for.
“Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3) — labour, not legislation.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the standard no council replaces.

pos: n. (c. 1046–1117, hermit of the forest of Craon and founder of the abbey and order of Tiron)
etymology: Bernard, from Germanic bern, bear, and hard, hardy; of Tiron in the Perche.
biblical_def: Bernard was a monk of Saint-Cyprien at Poitiers who twice abandoned office to live as a hermit in the forest of Craon, among a remarkable generation of solitary preachers that also produced Robert of Arbrissel and Vitalis of Savigny. In 1109 the count of the Perche gave him land at Tiron, where he founded an abbey that became the head of a small order with houses in France, Wales and Scotland. His distinctive policy was to receive craftsmen and to let them keep working at their trades inside the monastery, so that Tiron had its carpenters, smiths, masons, carvers and weavers rather than only its ploughmen. This dictionary records Bernard for that policy, because Scripture treats skilled handwork as a gift of God's own Spirit and not as a concession. The craftsmen of the tabernacle were filled for the purpose, “I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exo 31:3), and were given the ability to teach it on, “he hath put in his heart that he may teach” (Exo 35:34). The Lord himself worked a trade, “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary” (Mar 6:3), and an apostle kept one, “by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a craftsman as one skilled in a manual occupation; a trade as the business which a man has learned; workmanship as the skill of a workman; an artificer as one who makes by art; and handicraft as manual occupation.
webster_full: CRAFTSMAN, n. An artificer; a mechanic; one skilled in a manual occupation.
TRADE, n. The business which a person has learned and which he carries on for procuring subsistence or for profit; occupation.
WORKMANSHIP, n. The skill of a workman; the execution or manner of making any thing; that which is effected or produced.
ARTIFICER, n. An artist; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge of a particular kind.
HANDICRAFT, n. Manual occupation; work performed by the hand; also, a man who obtains his living by manual labor.
scriptures: Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
And he hath put in his heart that he may teach, both he, and Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.
Mar 6:3
Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us? And they were offended at him.
Act 18:3
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
corruption_summary: Hermit of Craon and founder of Tiron, c. 1046–1117: took in craftsmen and let them keep their trades, which Scripture calls a gift of the Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the standing of skilled work. The first man in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God is a craftsman, and the filling is explicitly for workmanship, “in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exo 31:3). The same passage makes the teaching of a trade a gift put in the heart, “he hath put in his heart that he may teach” (Exo 35:34). Tiron's smiths and carvers were not second-class monks.

The live corruption is the modern habit of ranking work by how clean the hands stay, which a church inherits whenever it treats a trade as what a man does until he can do something spiritual. The Lord of glory was known in his own village by his trade, “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary” (Mar 6:3), and the apostle to the Gentiles supported himself by stitching tents, “by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3). A dictionary that honours scriptoria should honour forges.
